title: Nullity, Basis & Dimension
subtitle: Nullity measures how many free variables a homogeneous system has. Rank + Nullity = number of columns — this is the rank-nullity theorem. Basis and dimension describe the structure of vector spaces: a basis is the minimal set of independent vectors that generates the whole space, and dimension is how many you need.
learningOutcome: Nullity measures how many free variables a homogeneous system has. Rank + Nullity = number of columns — this is the rank-nullity theorem. Basis and dimension describe the structure of vector spaces: a basis is the minimal set of independent vectors that generates the whole space, and dimension is how many you need.

content.text: After row reduction, zero rows = free variables. Nullity counts exactly those free variables. The rank-nullity theorem: rank + nullity = number of columns (not rows — columns).

items: Rank(A) + Nullity(A) = n where n = number of COLUMNS Nullity(A) = n - Rank(A)

content.text: Critical: n is the column count. Using row count instead is the most common error on this topic.
A = [ 1 3 4 3 ] ← 3 rows [ 3 9 12 9 ] ← 4 columns ← this is n [-1 3 4 1 ] n = 4 (we use this in rank-nullity)

R₂' = R₂ - 3·R₁: [3-3, 9-9, 12-12, 9-9] = [0, 0, 0, 0] → entire zero row R₃' = R₃ + R₁: [-1+1, 3+3, 4+4, 1+3] = [0, 6, 8, 4] After reduction: [ 1 3 4 3 ] [ 0 0 0 0 ] ← zero row [ 0 6 8 4 ] Swap R₂ and R₃: [ 1 3 4 3 ] [ 0 6 8 4 ] [ 0 0 0 0 ] ← zero row Non-zero rows = 2 → Rank = 2
Rank + Nullity = n 2 + Nullity = 4 Nullity = 2 This means: AX = 0 has 2 free variables. The homogeneous solution space has dimension 2.
Common mistake — Using rows instead of columns: students write nullity = 3 − 2 = 1. Wrong. The theorem uses columns: nullity = 4 − 2 = 2. The matrix has 3 rows, 4 columns. Always count columns for n.

content.text: A basis is any set of vectors that is (1) linearly independent — none can be built from the others — and (2) spans the space — every vector can be built from them. Dimension = number of vectors in any basis (always the same regardless of which basis you pick).
Standard basis of R², R³ — decomposing any vector
Why this is a valid basis — checking both conditions

Condition 1 (Independent): Can e₁ be built from e₂ and e₃? a·(0,1,0) + b·(0,0,1) = (0, a, b) For this to equal (1,0,0): need first entry = 1, impossible. → e₁, e₂, e₃ are independent ✓ Condition 2 (Spans R³): any (x,y,z) = x·e₁ + y·e₂ + z·e₃ ✓

Common mistake — Thinking there's only one basis for a vector space. Any 3 linearly independent vectors in R³ form a valid basis — not just e₁, e₂, e₃. What is fixed is the dimension (3). Examiners may ask you to find "a basis", not "the basis".
Connects directly to Week 10: eigenvectors form a basis for eigenspaces, and the dimension of each eigenspace determines whether a matrix is diagonalisable.
